analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government-run national health service providing free care to all residents.
analysis.headline: A single-payer bill to provide free health care to everyone in the United States was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to three House committees, and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have abolished the current health insurance system and created a United States Health Service, run by a National Health Board, that would provide comprehensive medical care — doctor visits, hospital care, dental, vision, drugs, mental health, and long-term care — free of charge to everyone in the country. Care would come from government-run facilities staffed by salaried health workers, financed by a new tax on individual and corporate income. It included strong patient rights, paid leave for medical appointments, and conflict-of-interest bans for health board members. It was never seriously considered: no other member of the House signed on, and it died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Every person living in the United States — including the uninsured, people with preexisting conditions, and the 40+ million without financial coverage cited in the bill's findings — would receive comprehensive care free at the point of service, paid for through progressive taxes on individuals and corporations. Health workers would become salaried federal-style employees with guaranteed employment, collective bargaining rights, and student loan repayment.

how_it_helps.text: It entitled every person in the United States to comprehensive health care — including dental, vision, mental health, prescription drugs, and long-term care — with no charge and no discrimination based on income, health status, or preexisting conditions.

It gave patients enforceable rights: free choice of providers and facilities, informed consent, confidentiality, grievance procedures with access to lawyers, and the right to appeal any denial or delay of care.
It amended federal labor law to give every worker one hour of paid leave for every 35 hours worked to use for their own or a dependent's health care, without losing pay.
It funded free education for health workers through service obligation, with the Service paying off student loans for those who joined, and guaranteed displaced insurance workers retraining.
It aimed to redistribute care to underserved rural, inner-city, and minority populations and to fund the system through progressive taxation rather than premiums tied to employment.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and corporations through a new health services tax on income, replacing private premiums and employer health benefits; private health insurers, for-profit hospitals, and fee-for-service providers would see their current business eliminated, with existing insurers' employees offered retraining.

drawbacks.text: It created a new tax on individual and corporate income to fund the system, meaning taxpayers would pay for universal care through the IRS rather than through premiums — a large, visible increase in taxes whose total cost was never scored publicly.

It gave a federal National Health Board sweeping control over hospitals, staffing, wages, and the building of facilities, including authority to take land by eminent domain, concentrating enormous power over one-sixth of the economy in a new unelected agency.

It effectively eliminated the private health insurance industry and the fee-for-service practice of medicine, forcing all providers into salaried government employment — a transition that would have disrupted existing employer-based coverage and the livelihoods of administrative staff (the bill set aside only up to 1% of the budget for two years to retrain displaced insurance workers).
It required health school graduates to work years in assigned locations as a condition of their free education, a service obligation some would consider coercive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was universal, no-charge comprehensive care financed by progressive taxes, which would have eliminated premiums, deductibles, and medical debt for tens of millions of Americans. The costs and risks were real: it centralized health care delivery in one federal agency, funded it with new taxes on individuals and corporations, and created a massive transition from employer-based insurance to government employment. It offered no experimental evidence for operating a system of this scale, and disruption during the transition would have been substantial. As a policy design, it was an ambitious single-payer model whose merits were never weighed by a committee or a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: A first-term bill with no cosponsors got referred to three committees and died there when the Congress ended, never reaching a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Barbara Lee introduced the bill on June 23, 2009, and it was referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor.
On June 24, 2009, the day after introduction, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health — and no further action was ever taken.
The bill sat without committee action for the rest of the 111th Congress and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

During the same period, Congress instead passed the Affordable Care Act of 2010, which expanded coverage through private insurance rather than replacing it — a widely reported fact that contextualizes why a government-run health service had no path forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, hospital systems, and drug companies, whose role in the health system continued unchanged; members of Congress also avoided a vote on a government takeover of health care.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 23, 2009 and advocated for a government-run national health service.

sides.party_line_note: With no cosponsors and no committee or floor action, no one in Congress other than the sponsor ever took a position on the record.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced employer-based and individual insurance entirely with a government health service, eliminating the industry's core business. It set aside only up to 1% of the Service budget for two years to retrain displaced insurance clerical and administrative workers.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital systems and physician practices billing private insurers
industries.note: All health workers would have become salaried government employees barred from private fee-for-service delivery, and the Service could acquire facilities by eminent domain. This threatened concentrated revenue in exchange for guaranteed employment in the Service.

The government would be the sole purchaser and distributor of drugs and devices through a national formulary, replacing fragmented private payment with one price-setting buyer — a large loss of pricing power, though sales volume would remain.

industries.industry: Health professions students and low-income patients
industries.note: Students would receive free education with loans repaid in exchange for service; patients would receive care free at the point of service. Not a conventional industry, but these groups bore concentrated stakes in the bill's fate.
